title: Claims-Based Authorization
description: Use claims-based authorization for fine-grained, attribute-based access control in modern applications.

data.text: **Claims-Based Authorization** takes a more granular approach than roles. Instead of asking "what role does this user have?", it asks "what specific attributes or capabilities does this user possess?" A claim is a statement about a user - such as their department, clearance level, or subscription tier.

While roles are coarse-grained categories, claims are fine-grained attributes. A user with the 'Editor' role might have claims like `Department: Marketing`, `ClearanceLevel: 3`, and `CanPublish: true`. This allows you to build authorization logic that goes far beyond simple role checks.

cards.title: Roles
cards.description: Group users into categories for broad access control.

cards.title: Claims
cards.description: Attribute-based statements about users for fine-grained control.

data.title: Standard and Custom Claims
items: **Name / Email**: Basic identity claims (often in JWT 'sub' claim)
**Department**: Marketing, Engineering, Sales - used for data isolation
**ClearanceLevel**: Numeric or string value for security classification

data.text: Claims are added to a user's identity when they are created or updated. ASP.NET Core Identity uses the `UserClaimsPrincipalFactory` to transform a `User` and their claims into a `ClaimsPrincipal`. You can also add claims directly during JWT token generation.

data.title: Adding Claims During User Creation
Protecting Endpoints with Claims
Never Trust Client-Provided Claims
data.text: Claims in JWTs are base64-encoded, not encrypted. An attacker can modify and re-sign tokens if they know your secret. Always validate claims server-side and never rely solely on client-provided values for authorization decisions.

ASP.NET Core provides two primary ways to use claims for authorization: the `[Authorize]` attribute with policy names (which we cover in the next lesson) and direct claim checks using `User.FindFirst()` or `User.HasClaim()`. For simple scenarios, direct checks work well. For complex rules, policy-based authorization is preferred.

data.title: Direct Claim Checks

data.text: When using JWT authentication in React, claims are embedded in the token payload. You decode the token client-side to access claims for UI decisions. However, always remember that client-side decisions are convenience features - the real authorization must happen on the server.

data.title: Decoding JWT Claims in React
Use a Claims Transformer for Dynamic Claims
data.text: If claims change frequently (like subscription status), implement a `IClaimsTransformation` service in ASP.NET Core to dynamically augment the user's claims principal on each request.

data.caption: Claims-based authorization decision flow
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[User Authenticates] --> B[Identity Issues Claims]
    B --> C[Claims in JWT / Cookie]
    C --> D[Request with Claims]
    D --> E{Has Required Claim?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Allow Access]
    E -->|No| G[Check Other Conditions]
    G --> H{Pass?}
    H -->|Yes| F
    H -->|No| I[403 Forbidden]

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Claims are fine-grained attributes about a user
Use claims for scenarios where roles are too coarse
Claims work excellently with JWT tokens
Use [Authorize] with policies for complex claim rules
data.takeaway: Claims provide the flexibility needed for modern, attribute-based access control.
